question.problem:
Suppose that for the angles $u$ and $v,$ we have

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡u=\frac{7}{25},\,\operatorname{cos}⁡u=\frac{24}{25},\,\operatorname{cos}⁡v=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.
$$

Given that both $u$ and $v$ lie in the first quadrant, then

| $\operatorname{cos}⁡(u-v)$ | $=$ | {{field-1}} $\sqrt{3}\,+\,$ {{field-2}} |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  |  | $50$ |
question.worked_solution:
First, we recall the difference formula for cosine:

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡(u-v)=\operatorname{cos}⁡u\operatorname{cos}⁡v+\operatorname{sin}⁡u\operatorname{sin}⁡v
$$

We know the values of $\operatorname{sin}⁡u$, $\operatorname{cos}⁡u$, and $\operatorname{cos}⁡v.$ To find the missing value of $\operatorname{sin}⁡v,$ we can use the Pythagorean identity:

$$
{sin}^{2}⁡v+{cos}^{2}⁡v=1\,⟹\,{sin}^{2}⁡v=1-{cos}^{2}⁡v
$$

Substituting our values into the Pythagorean identity, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡v & =1-{cos}^{2}⁡v \\  & =1-{(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})}^{2} \\  & =1-\frac{(\sqrt{3})^{2}}{{2}^{2}} \\  & =1-\frac{3}{4} \\  & =\frac{4}{4}-\frac{3}{4} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡v & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{1}{4}} \\  & =\pm \frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $v$ lies in the first quadrant, where sine is positive, we take

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡v=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

We can now apply the difference formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(u-v) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡u\operatorname{cos}⁡v+\operatorname{sin}⁡u\operatorname{sin}⁡v \\  & =(\frac{24}{25})(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})+(\frac{7}{25})(\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =\frac{24\sqrt{3}}{50}+\frac{7}{50} \\  & =\frac{24\sqrt{3}+7}{50}\end{aligned}
$$
